body: Most utility poles in Mexico are made of concrete and have an octagonal shape, often with engravings on the side. Note that octagonal poles are also common in Colombia.
Mexico uses short licence plates with a large variety of designs, and front plates are required. For an overview of the most common regional designs, see step 2.
The most typical Mexican road lines are solid white outer lines with a single unbroken yellow middle line. However, single broken and double yellow middle lines are also common.
Small, cylindrical white bollards with a black base are unique to Mexico. A yellow reflector can sometimes be seen, and a flat version also exists.
Mexico has two main road shields: one for national highways with "MEXICO" at the top and a curvy design, and one for state roads with straight borders and state initials at the top.
Mexican directional signs have a distinctly large, all-caps white font.
Mexican kilometre markers are white, with black font and outline.
Cacti of many different species are extremely common in Mexico.
Mexico uses the word “ALTO” on stop signs, whereas all of South America uses “PARE”.
Arrows on signs are noticeably very thick.
Yellow accents on kerbs and bridge barriers are quite common.
You will commonly see wide cylindrical, black or white water tanks on rooftops.
OXXO and Pemex are two of the most popular gas station brands in Mexico. While less common, OXXO can still be found in other countries.
Many place names in Mexico are of Nahuatl origin, featuring a lot of ‘x’ and ‘tl’, as well as ‘-ec’ and ‘-tlan’ suffixes.
Mexico uses circular electricity counters. These are not unique to Mexico and can also be found in the US, Guatemala, Dominican Republic, and the Philippines.
United States car brands are popular in Mexico, and you will see a lot of pickup trucks in particular.
Mexico is one of the few Latin American countries with Generation 2 coverage. Brazil has some, but it is much rarer.

Generation 3 coverage in Mexico mainly features two cars: a white car with a stubby antenna with a diagonal coil, or a white car with a more visible back and a long red brake light instead of an antenna. It is also possible to find a white car with a tiny sliver visible where the antenna should be.
The Generation 4 cars in Mexico commonly have a visible front and come in various colours. The three most common are blue, white with a blue stripe, and black.
The first digit of Mexican area codes are regional and can be identified using the provided map.
Mexican postal codes can be identified using the provided map. They often appear at the bottom of street signs and are ordered alphabetically by state name.
Mexican postal codes commonly appear at the bottom of street signs and are ordered alphabetically by state name.
Each Mexican state has unique licence plate designs, which can be helpful for region-guessing.
Prickly pear cacti, with their flat oval pads, are most common in central Mexico and rare in southern and coastal areas.
Pulque agaves have wide, curling leaves and a crown-like look, found in the central valley and near San Luis Potosi.
Vast fields of blue agave, used for tequila, are mostly found in the states of Jalisco and Nayarit.
Tree yuccas have sharp, green leaf rosettes on a trunk and are most common in San Luis Potosi and Zacatecas.
The Mexican Giant Cardon cactus, with its large sprawling arms and ribbed exterior, is extremely common in the Baja California peninsula.
The Saguaro Cactus, featuring short curving arms from a main trunk, is found in the western half of Sonora.
Organ Pipe Cacti have long, thin stems growing from ground level and are mostly found in Sonora and occasionally Baja California Sur.
The Blue Myrtle Cactus, with short arms curving uniformly upwards, is abundant in San Luis Potosi and also found in Queretaro and Hidalgo.
Sugar cane is found throughout Mexico but is most common in the state of Veracruz.
Coconut palms are found along the coast, with large groups common in Guerrero and Colima.
Sabal palms, with a spiky, sun-shaped crown giving a lollipop-like appearance, are common on the east coast, the Yucatan peninsula, and in Nayarit.
The Attalea rostrata is a huge palm with upright, umbrella-like leaves, mostly exclusive to Veracruz and Tabasco.
Oil palm plantations are most common in Chiapas and can also be found in neighboring states.
Boojum trees, known for their alien, tentacle-like appearance, are almost exclusively found in the southern half of Baja California.
Brittlebush are small shrubs with bright silver-grey leaves, most common in Sonora, especially around Hermosillo.
Thin, white-barked trees are found in the Yucatan peninsula, but are most prevalent in Quintana Roo.
Golden tufts of grass in a line next to the road are a common sight in Coahuila.
Clumps of grass in a teardrop shape are common in the region around Tlaxcala.
Red agricultural fields are commonly seen in Zacatecas and occasionally southern Durango.
The Monterrey metropolitan area is surrounded by tall, stunning mountain ranges.

The western parts of Chihuahua and Durango can feature a rocky mountainous landscape covered with pine forests. These pines are generally shorter and more stunted in appearance than pine forests of the central or south.
Extremely dark fields are common in Guanajuato.
These reddish brown-tinged hills, often accompanied by large boulders, are a common sight for the northern half of Baja California.
Almost blindingly white soil in the Yucatan peninsula is most common in Quintana Roo. NOTE: This is only consistent in Generation 3.
These red agricultural fields surrounded by dense forests of tropical trees are most common in northern Campeche.
Red brick buildings are mostly concentrated in the states west of Mexico City, specifically Jalisco, Michoacan, Guanajuato, and Aguascalientes.
White concrete block buildings are highly concentrated in the states surrounding Mexico city, and are generally more common to the east. They can however still be found all over the country.
Mud brick buildings are most abundant in Durango, especially full houses constructed with mud brick. However, they can essentially be found in almost all of the dry desert states.

Architecture in northern Mexico often features design elements from American style bungalows. Many houses are coloured with light or pastel colours, gated and commonly have front yards. Orange tiles inspired by Spanish colonial architecture are also typical.
Thatched roofs are most common in the Yucatan peninsula and eastern San Luis Potosi. They can also be found elsewhere, mainly in the southeast.
These walls made of light coloured rock are found in the Yucatan peninsula, but most common in Yucatan state.
A thick cross can be seen on the back of signs in Chihuahua.
Bollards with a red band near the top are unique to Nayarit, apart from one exception being Federal Highway 190 on the Oaxaca-Chiapas border.
Jalisco bollards will sometimes have a crown and the text ‘Jalisco’ written on it. These are usually barely legible unless very close, however no other Mexican bollard will have writing on it.
White insulators that are shaped like acorns can be found along the coastal states of Mexico, but are by far most common in Michoacan, Colima, and Veracruz.
Poles with an asymmetric crossbar and double-stacked insulators are exclusive to Mexico City, State of Mexico, Hidalgo, and Morelos.
Wooden poles with a lowered crossbar are mostly found in Sinaloa and Sonora.
These concrete poles with insulators suspended below the crossbars are unique to the Yucatan peninsula.
The wooden variant of the hanging pole is found on the Baja California peninsula.
Poles with a lowered crossbar and a single support beam that extend from one end of the crossbar to the pole itself can be found in Durango.
Poles with a mesh body are most commonly found in San Luis Potosi, Guanajuato, and Queretaro.
White middle road lines are most commonly found in Tabasco.
Fences made of trees with red-coloured bark are commonly found in Veracruz. However, they can also appear in other coastal states, so it's best to use this clue in combination with others.
Black tar on both sides of the yellow center line is a clue for Sinaloa, Durango, and Guerrero. This meta is most reliable when the tar is not faded.
Grainy pavement with a blue-ish grey tinge is common in Tamaulipas and Nuevo Leon. In Tamaulipas, larger roads often have dashed outer lines.
Unorganized cobblestone pavement with irregular tiles is a strong indicator for the central states of Nayarit, Jalisco, Colima, and Queretaro.
Pavement made of hexagonal tiles is a clue for Puebla and Tlaxcala.
A specific pavement design with three lines of cobblestone patterning is primarily found in Oaxaca.
Taxis in and around Mexico City are distinctively colored with a white lower half and a pink upper half.
The Mexicali area has flat farmland with a ridge to the west. Look for common Washingtonia palms and brown wooden poles.
The area around Poza Rica in Veracruz is known for its many citrus tree plantations, often grown on hillsides.
Ciudad Obregon is recognizable by its distinctive pinkish-tan soil and the presence of canals in its agricultural areas.
The twin volcanoes of Iztaccíhuatl and Popocatépetl are located on the border of the State of Mexico and Puebla. They are often not as clear as in pictures.
Cerro del Bernal is a distinctive extinct volcano in southern Tamaulipas. You can spot it northwest of Tampico.
An extremely long and flat ridge is a key feature of the Sierra del Abra Tanchipa Biosphere Reserve in eastern San Luis Potosi.
A tall, flat ridge with prominent ridgelines can be seen from Highway 53 in Northern Coahuila, part of the Maderas del Carmen Biosphere Reserve.
The outskirts of Ciudad Juárez are characterized by dirt roads with a distinct shade of orange soil and low shrubs.
In Oaxaca, near San Cristóbal Suchixtlahuaca, the rolling hills have distinctive orange and beige-tinged soil that alternates from hill to hill.
The town of Guaymas is recognizable by its many jagged cliffs and mountains, pinkish soil, and scattered organ-pipe cacti.
The town of Los Coloradas is famous for the pink lakes surrounding it.
Highway 54 in northeastern Zacatecas is a divided highway lined with numerous yucca trees. The Street View car often appears overexposed and almost white.
Highway 40D crossing the Sinaloa-Durango border features stunning lush cliffs and mountains, frequent tunnels, and double yellow middle road lines.
A road divider with a yellow top and bottom edge is found along the entire 95D highway from Mexico City to Acapulco.
Rows of wind turbines from the Eurus Wind Farm, Mexico's largest, can be seen along Highway 190 in southeast Oaxaca near Juchitán de Zaragoza.
Most lamp posts and lamp arms in Aguascalientes city are yellow, though this is a common feature and not exclusive.
A lamp with a black rectangular head is a clue for Cuernavaca.
In Santiago de Queretaro, look for lamps with black front and back edges and a white middle section.
A distinctive lamp with five circular bulbs, resembling a dice, is found in Cancun.
In Matamoros, you can find lamps with a rectangular head and a ring-shaped light bulb.
A lamp with a zig-zag bent pole arm is a feature of Hermosillo.
The bottom half of utility poles in Cuernavaca are often painted green. The paint may appear faded in Generation 4 coverage.
In Chihuahua city, poles sometimes have a strip of white paint with the street name written on it.
A Street View car with a yellow hood is visible near the La Malinche volcano in Tlaxcala.
A white truck with visible rearview mirrors is the Street View vehicle in the Cofre de Perote national park.
A red Street View car with a black roof is found in the town of La Seca in Sinaloa.
